blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 19 (Chromosome and DNA), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the chemical composition of a chromosome. Explain the levels of organization by which DNA is packed into a chromatid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chemical composition: a chromosome is made of 40% DNA and 60% proteins (histones). Both chromatids have identical DNA. The DNA of an average human chromosome is about 5 cm long with about 140 million nucleotides. DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups) and histones are positively charged (rich in arginine and lysine), so DNA has strong affinity for histones.

Levels of organization:
1. Nucleosome string: about every 146 nucleotides of DNA (2 nm thick) wrap twice around a histone octamer (two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) to form a nucleosome. Nucleosomes are joined by about 80 nucleotide long linker DNA; the linker histone H1 sits near the DNA entry and exit points and helps winding. The nucleosomes look like beads on a string, the nucleosome string (11 nm).
2. Chromatin fibre: in early cell division the nucleosome string coils again about its axis; tightly packed nucleosomes make the chromatin fibre (30 nm).
3. Supercoil and chromatid: the chromatin fibre folds upon itself into a supercoil (300 nm), which further coils and condenses into a chromatid (700 nm).

book_ref.quote: The following are the levels of the organization of chromosomes

blocks.prompt: 2 A genetic material must have certain characteristics. (i) State these characteristics. (ii) Explain how Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identified the transforming principle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Characteristics of a genetic material:
1. It must be able to code for the sequence of amino acids in proteins.
2. It must be able to replicate itself prior to cell division.
3. It must be in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.
4. It must be able to change over time to account for evolution.
Only DNA fulfils all these requirements.

(ii) Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944):
1. They removed proteins from dead S-type bacteria and mixed them with live R-type. Mice injected with this mixture developed disease and live S-type bacteria were found in them, so proteins are not responsible for transforming R-type into S-type.
2. They then removed all DNA from dead S-type, mixed it with live R-type and injected mice. No transformation occurred and the mice remained healthy.
They concluded that DNA is the fundamental unit of the transforming principle.

book_ref.quote: Only one molecule i.e., DNA fulfils all these requirements

blocks.prompt: 3 Compare the experiment of Griffith with the experiment of Hershey and Chase. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both experiments dealt with the hereditary material, but they differed as follows.

book_ref.quote: Based on these observations, Hershey and Chase claimed that the DNA of bacteriophages

rows: Performed in 1928 by Fredrick Griffith
Performed in 1952 by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase

Used bacteriophages (with DNA) infecting bacteria
Used heat-killed S-type mixed with live R-type
Used radioactive tracers: ³⁵S for protein and ³²P for DNA

³⁵S stayed in the medium; ³²P entered the bacterial cells

blocks.prompt: 4 Radio-isotopes are used to trace DNA in experiments. (i) What is a pulse-chase experiment? (ii) How did Meselson and Stahl prepare heavy DNA and separate DNA molecules of different densities? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Pulse-chase experiment: an experiment in which radio-isotope labelled DNA is traced in the progeny of an organism. It has two stages:
1. Pulse: the organism is exposed to the radio-isotope for a brief time and incorporates it into its DNA.
2. Chase: the labelled DNA is observed over time by measuring its radioactivity.

(ii) Meselson and Stahl:
1. They grew bacteria in a medium with the heavy isotope ¹⁵N; after many generations the DNA had ¹⁵N in its nitrogen bases and was denser than normal.
2. They transferred these bacteria to a ¹⁴N medium, so new DNA would be made with ¹⁴N, and collected DNA at intervals (0, 20 and 40 minutes).
3. The DNA was dissolved in aqueous cesium chloride and ultracentrifuged. This created a cesium density gradient (denser cesium at the bottom).
4. Each DNA settled where its density exactly matched the cesium density there; the denser ¹⁵N DNA migrated further down than the lighter ¹⁴N DNA.

book_ref.quote: They checked heavier DNA (with ¹⁵N) and lighter DNA (with ¹⁴N)

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the roles of the enzymes and proteins that work in DNA replication in prokaryotes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Initiator protein: binds to the replication origin site and initiates the process.
2. Helicases: unwinding enzymes that break the hydrogen bonds between the base-pairs, forming two replication forks (a replication bubble).
3. Gyrase (topoisomerase): attaches ahead of the replication fork and prevents the supercoiling produced by unwinding.
4. Single-strand binding proteins: bind the single strands and prevent them from re-joining and rewinding.
5. Primase: attaches a primer of 5-10 RNA nucleotides in front of each template strand at the origin.
6. DNA polymerase III: the main enzyme; matches free nucleotides to the template (A with T, C with G), adding them only to the 3′ end, in the 5′ to 3′ direction; it makes the continuous leading strand and the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand, and proofreads.
7. DNA polymerase I: at termination removes the RNA primers and fills the gaps (also between Okazaki fragments) with DNA nucleotides.
8. DNA ligase: joins the Okazaki fragments of the lagging strand.
(DNA polymerase II repairs DNA damage during the life of the cell.)

book_ref.quote: The enzyme gyrase (or topoisomerase) attaches ahead of the replication fork

blocks.prompt: 6 Compare DNA replication in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The basic mechanism is similar in all organisms, but the following differences exist.

book_ref.quote: Prokaryotes replicate their small DNA very quickly

rows: Location: cytoplasm (no nucleus)
Location: nucleus
DNA polymerase I, II and III work
At least 14 polymerases (e.g. alpha, delta, epsilon)
Single origin site and single termination site
Multiple origin and termination sites on each chromosome; several replicons
Okazaki fragments longer (1000-2000 nucleotides)
Okazaki fragments short (100-200 nucleotides)
Small DNA replicated very quickly
Massive linear DNA: replication starts at thousands of origin sites at the same time

blocks.prompt: 7 Replicating DNA has two important properties. (i) Explain the stability and variability of DNA. (ii) Describe how biotechnologists use DNA replication. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Stability means the ability of DNA to be copied with accuracy. DNA polymerase III (and eukaryotic polymerases) have a proofreading ability that maintains the nucleotide sequence; this maintains the specific traits of an organism and ensures cells function correctly.
Variability is the exception: occasionally a permanent change in DNA sequence, a mutation, occurs, due to replication errors or environmental factors. Variability is the primary source of new traits; it lets populations adapt to changing environments and is the raw material for evolution.

(ii) Uses of DNA replication:
1. PCR: replication is conducted to make billions of copies of a specific DNA.
2. Recombinant DNA technology: DNA cut from different sources is replicated to amplify it.
3. Genome sequencing: multiple copies of the genome are made and then sequenced.
4. Diagnostic studies: specific sections of a patient's DNA are replicated and searched for mutations to detect a genetic disorder.

book_ref.quote: These are two important properties of a replicating DNA

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe how the genetic code was worked out by Francis Crick, Marshall Nirenberg, Philip Leder and Har Gobind Khorana. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Francis Crick (1961): he and his colleagues proposed that the genetic code is a series of blocks called codons, each specifying one amino acid. If single nucleotides specified amino acids, only 4 could be encoded; 2-nucleotide codons would give only 16 (4 × 4). So a codon must be 3 nucleotides: 4 nucleotides give 64 (4 × 4 × 4) triplets, more than enough for 20 amino acids. The code is a triplet code; DNA codons are transcribed as complementary mRNA codons (TAC on DNA = AUG on mRNA).

Marshall Nirenberg (1961): he made a poly-U mRNA (only uracil) and added it to the cytoplasm of bacteria; they made a polypeptide of many phenylalanines, so UUU specifies phenylalanine.

Nirenberg and Philip Leder tested all triplet codons and determined the amino acids of 47 codons. Har Gobind Khorana (who studied at Government College, Lahore) determined the remaining 17.

Result: of the 64 codons, UGA, UAG and UAA are stop (nonsense) codons and AUG is the start codon, specifying methionine.

book_ref.quote: Nirenberg and another American geneticist Philip Leder tested all triplet codons

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the characteristics of the genetic code. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Universal: the code is the same in almost all organisms; e.g. AGA specifies arginine in bacteria, humans and all others, so genes can be transferred among organisms. Exceptions: mitochondrial DNA uses a slightly different code (reflecting its independent evolutionary history), and some ciliates and viruses use different codes.
2. Triplet: each codon is a sequence of three nucleotides, so the information in DNA balances that needed to specify 20 kinds of amino acids.
3. Degenerate: multiple codons can specify the same amino acid, e.g. GUU, GUC, GUA and GUG all code for valine. This is important for mutation tolerance and evolutionary flexibility.
4. Without punctuation: a codon is read continuously, with no gaps between its three nucleotides.
5. Non-overlapping: each triplet is read independently of adjacent codons; AUGAGCGCA is read only as AUG/AGC/GCA, not AUG/UGA/GAG.

book_ref.quote: Characteristic is important for mutation tolerance and evolutionary flexibility

blocks.prompt: 10 Transcription begins when RNA polymerase binds a promoter. (i) Name the promoters of prokaryotes and eukaryotes with their positions. (ii) Describe the subunits of RNA polymerase and how the transcription bubble is formed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) A promoter is a special nucleotide sequence on template DNA where RNA polymerase binds; it is not itself transcribed (no primer is needed).
Prokaryotes: TTGACA, 35 nucleotides before the start point (–35 sequence); TATAAT, 10 nucleotides before the start point (–10 sequence).
Eukaryotes: TATAAA (TATA box), 25 nucleotides before the start point (–25 sequence); GGCCAATCT (CAAT box), 70 nucleotides before (–70 sequence).

(ii) RNA polymerase has five subunits:
1. Two α subunits bind with regulatory proteins.
2. A β′ subunit binds with template DNA.
3. A β subunit binds with RNA nucleotides.
4. A σ subunit recognizes the promoter and initiates synthesis.
When RNA polymerase attaches to the promoter, its σ subunit is removed. The other four subunits (core enzyme) unwind the DNA helix and break the base-pairs, forming a bubble-like structure, the transcription bubble, in which the RNA chain is assembled.

book_ref.quote: RNA polymerase consists of five subunits

blocks.prompt: 11 Compare DNA replication with transcription. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both processes copy information from a DNA template, but they differ as follows.

book_ref.quote: During transcription, a complementary RNA is synthesised from DNA

rows: DNA makes an identical copy of itself
A complementary RNA is made from DNA
Both strands are copied
Only the template strand is transcribed
Main enzyme: DNA polymerase III (with helicase, primase, ligase etc.)
Enzyme: RNA polymerase
Needs an RNA primer made by primase
No primer is needed; RNA polymerase binds a promoter
Raw materials: deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP)
Raw materials: ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTP)
Occurs in the S-phase of interphase, before cell division
First step of gene expression

blocks.prompt: 12 Translation needs activated amino acids and a ribosome. (i) What is the activation of amino acids? (ii) Describe the initiation complex and the three sites of the ribosome. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Activation of amino acids: before protein synthesis, specific tRNAs attach with specific amino acids to make aminoacyl-tRNAs (aa-tRNA). The enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase does this; there are 20 kinds, each binding a specific amino acid and recognizing the tRNA with anticodons for it. The aa-tRNA delivers the amino acid to the ribosome.

(ii) Initiation complex: the aa-tRNA with the first amino acid binds the smaller ribosomal subunit (controlled by an initiation factor); another initiation factor attaches the 5′ end of mRNA to the small subunit and places the anticodon over the first codon (AUG); then the larger subunit is placed on it. The complex consists of both ribosomal subunits, the first aa-tRNA, mRNA and the enzyme.
Sites of the ribosome:
1. P site (peptidyl site): where peptide bonds form between amino acids; holds the first aa-tRNA.
2. A site (aminoacyl site): where the next aa-tRNA binds.
3. E site (exit site): where empty tRNAs exit.
With respect to mRNA they are arranged 5′ to 3′ as E-P-A, because ribosomes move toward the 3′ end.

book_ref.quote: The aa-tRNA delivers the amino acid to the ribosome for incorporation into the polypeptide chain

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe the roles of the enzymes and protein factors that work during translation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (20 kinds): attaches each specific amino acid to its tRNA, forming aa-tRNA (activation of amino acids).
2. Initiation factors: one controls the binding of the first aa-tRNA to the smaller ribosomal subunit; another attaches the 5′ end of mRNA to the small subunit and positions the anticodon over the start codon AUG.
3. Elongation factor: helps the next aa-tRNA with a matching anticodon bind to the A site.
4. Peptidyl transferase: removes the amino acid (first, methionine) from the tRNA at the P site and joins it by a peptide bond to the amino acid at the A site. The ribosome then moves three nucleotides (translocation); the steps repeat until a stop codon reaches the A site.
5. Release factor: a protein that recognizes the stop codon at the A site and releases the polypeptide from the tRNA at the P site; the tRNA is released and ribosomal subunits separate from mRNA.

book_ref.quote: These steps are repeated again and again until the stop codon is reached at A site

blocks.prompt: 14 Gene expression is regulated in many ways. (i) At which levels is gene expression regulated? (ii) Explain how genes are regulated during splicing. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Regulation of gene expression occurs at several levels:
1. Transcriptional level: the rate of transcription is regulated (regulatory proteins bind regulatory sequences of genes; repressors bind operators and block RNA polymerase, activators help RNA polymerase bind the promoter).
2. Post-transcriptional level: the modification of mRNA is controlled.
3. Translational level: the rate of translation is regulated.
4. Post-translational level: the modification of protein (folding, stability etc.) is regulated.

(ii) Regulation during splicing: in eukaryotes mRNA is modified before export to the cytoplasm. Genes can be tuned ON or OFF during splicing (removal of introns and joining of exons). Specific regulatory proteins in specific cell types control splicing and remove pieces of mRNA (introns or exons) in different ways, so mRNAs of different lengths are produced. As a result more than one polypeptide is produced from a single gene (alternate splicing).

book_ref.quote: These proteins remove the pieces of mRNA (introns or exons) in different ways

blocks.prompt: 15 Define mutation. Explain natural and induced mutations, and how mutations contribute to evolution. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mutation: a change in the content of the genetic message. It may be small (a change in one or a few nucleotides) or large (a change in a large segment or a whole chromosome). Agents causing mutations are mutagens; the organism or cell with the mutation is a mutant.

Natural mutations occur spontaneously as a result of sequencing errors or DNA damage during replication. They are part of evolution and may be beneficial, neutral or harmful.
Induced mutations are caused by external factors: mutagen substances, radiation, environmental chemicals (certain pesticides, industrial pollutants) or medical treatments such as chemotherapy. They can have serious health effects.

Mutations and evolution: mutation and recombination are the ultimate sources of all genetic variation. They create new DNA sequences (alleles) and combinations of alleles, giving new traits that may be advantageous, harmful or neutral. Natural selection acts on these variations and the allele frequencies of advantageous traits increase, leading to evolution in the long run.

book_ref.quote: Induced mutations are caused by external factors such as exposure to mutagen substances or radiation

blocks.prompt: 16 Explain silent, missense and nonsense mutations with one example of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Silent mutations: do not change the amino acid sequence of the protein. Because of the degeneracy of the genetic code, the changed codon still specifies the same amino acid. Example: the mRNA codon GGC changing to GGU; both code for glycine.

2. Missense mutations: change only one amino acid, which can affect protein function. Example: a single nucleotide change (A to T) in the haemoglobin gene replaces glutamic acid by valine; red blood cells lose their round shape, causing sickle cell anaemia.

3. Nonsense mutations: create a premature stop codon, giving shortened, non-functional proteins. Example: in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy a nonsense mutation creates a premature stop signal in the middle of the gene; the short protein cannot function, causing progressive muscle weakness.

book_ref.quote: These mutations create a premature stop codon in the protein sequence

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the possible ways to treat genetic diseases. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Gene therapy: correcting or replacing the mutated gene with a functional gene.
2. Cell therapy: replacing non-functioning cells with healthy ones through transplantation. For example, in type 1 diabetes the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin do not function; cell therapy replaces them with healthy cells.
3. Pharmacogenomics: tailoring drug treatment to an individual's genetic makeup; by analysing a patient's DNA, doctors can identify the best drug for him.
4. Genetic counselling: for individuals with a family history of genetic diseases it provides information and support, including genetic testing, education on the disease, and guidance on family planning and reproductive options.

book_ref.quote: Possible ways to treat genetic diseases

blocks.prompt: 18 Compare sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria as disorders caused by point mutations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both are caused by single-gene (point) mutations and appear when a child receives both recessive alleles.

book_ref.quote: The following are two important genetic disorders caused by single-gene mutations

rows: Recessive gene of the abnormal β chain of haemoglobin on chromosome 11
Recessive allele of the gene for liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) on chromosome 12
Substitution: DNA nucleotide T replaced by A, so glutamic acid is replaced by valine
Point mutation (e.g. substitution or deletion) reduces PAH activity
Abnormal haemoglobin carries less oxygen; RBCs become sickle shaped
Phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine and builds up to toxic levels
Symptoms: pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, jaundice, more infections
Symptoms: intellectual disability, seizures, behavioural problems, microcephaly, musty odour; brain damage
Treatment: NSAIDs and opioids for pain, blood transfusions, bone marrow transplant (long-term cure), vaccinations and antibiotics
Management: avoid high-phenylalanine foods, monitor blood phenylalanine, nutritional supplements

blocks.prompt: 19 Describe the changes in chromosome structure: chromosomal rearrangements and insertional inactivation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chromosomal mutations are large-scale mutations involving changes in the position of genes or in the structure or number of chromosomes; they are usually spontaneous.

1. Chromosomal rearrangements: chromosomes can undergo physical alterations such as deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations. Usually these are caused by breakage of the DNA double helices at two different locations.
- Translocation: a segment of one chromosome becomes part of another chromosome.
- Inversion: the orientation of a portion of a chromosome is reversed.

2. Insertional inactivation: many small segments of chromosomes, called transposons or jumping genes, can move from one location to another in the genome, selecting new locations at random. Some are inserted into genes and inactivate them. This is common in nature, and many human gene disorders result from transposition. Example: a human transposon inserted into the clotting factor IX gene on the X chromosome places a stop codon in the middle of the gene, resulting in X-linked haemophilia.

book_ref.quote: Chromosomal Rearrangements: Chromosomes can undergo physical alterations

blocks.prompt: 20 What is non-disjunction? Explain how non-disjunction of sex chromosomes produces XXY, XXX, XO and OY zygotes, and the fate of each. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Non-disjunction: occasionally chromatids fail to separate properly in meiosis, so a gamete gains or loses a chromosome. If such a gamete forms a zygote, severe abnormalities can result. It can occur in autosomes or sex chromosomes.

Non-disjunction of X in the mother gives eggs with XX or with no sex chromosome (O):
1. XX egg + normal Y sperm → XXY (47; 44+XXY): Klinefelter syndrome, a sterile male. XXY can also arise when an XY sperm (non-disjunction in the father) fertilizes a normal X egg.
2. XX egg + X sperm → XXX (47): triple X syndrome, a fertile female with learning disabilities, tall stature and wide-spaced eyes.
3. O egg + normal X sperm (or O sperm + normal X egg) → XO (45; 44+XO): Turner syndrome, a sterile female (monosomy of sex chromosomes).
4. O egg + normal Y sperm → OY: the zygote fails to develop, because humans cannot survive without the genes on the X chromosome.

book_ref.quote: the egg may have both X chromosomes (XX) or may have no sex chromosome (designated as O)

blocks.prompt: 21 Abnormal chromosome numbers have different causes and outcomes. (i) Why is the age of the mother more critical than that of the father for non-disjunction? (ii) What is the fate of zygotes with one less or one extra autosome? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) There is a much greater chance of non-disjunction accumulating over time in eggs than in sperm. All future eggs have developed to prophase I by the time a female is born, so when she has children her eggs are as old as she is. Men, in contrast, produce new sperm daily. Therefore the age of the mother is more critical.

(ii) A zygote with one less autosome cannot complete development. Most zygotes with an extra autosome also do not survive. However, pairs 13, 15, 18, 21 and 22 can have three chromosomes and the individual can survive for a time:
- An extra chromosome in pair 13, 15 or 18 causes severe developmental defects; such infants die within a few months.
- Individuals with an extra chromosome 21 or 22 usually survive to adulthood, but their skeletal maturation is delayed, so they are generally short with poor muscles, and their mental development is affected (e.g. Down syndrome, trisomy 21).

book_ref.quote: If a zygote receives one less autosome, it cannot complete development
